core: what Homo sapiens is: the hominin species to which all living humans belong (working definition, attributed to Smithsonian Human Origins and OpenStax)
origins: anatomically modern humans appear in Africa — stated factually with attributed dates (Smithsonian ~300,000 years ago; OpenStax ~200,000 years ago)

dispersal: H. sapiens spread worldwide — stated factually, with the documented timeline (Asia 80,000–60,000; Australia by 50,000; Europe by 40,000; Americas by 15,000 years ago) and an original example of migration
encounters: interaction with other hominins, especially Neanderthals — stated factually, attributed; the honest note that some interbreeding occurred, per genetic evidence
capacities: symbolic culture, art, and complex language — each named with one line, stated factually
the honest note: all living humans are one species — the reality check, stated factually
the honest framing: our species is young, and the story is still being written — the reality check

H. sapiens became the sole surviving hominin as other species went extinct (Smithsonian)

claims.claim: Homo sapiens is the hominin species to which all living humans belong: the Smithsonian's Human Origins Program states that Homo sapiens is the species that all living human beings on the planet belong to, and its 'One Species, Living Worldwide' page presents all living humans as one species spread across the planet.

Anatomically modern humans originated in Africa: the Smithsonian dates the evolution of Homo sapiens to about 300,000 years ago in Africa during a time of dramatic climate change, while OpenStax's Introduction to Anthropology dates the first appearance of modern H. sapiens to about 200,000 years ago in Africa; both attribute the origin to Africa, and the lesson brackets the attributed dates.

Anatomically modern humans are characterized by brains averaging about 1,300 cubic centimeters, a high-vaulted skull with a flat, near-vertical forehead, reduced brow ridges, a lighter skeleton, and a projecting chin; OpenStax notes that modern H. sapiens is the first hominin to exhibit a projecting chin, and 'anatomically modern Homo sapiens' is the term for prehistoric members of the species whose bodies match modern humans but who lacked later cultural traditions.

Homo sapiens dispersed out of Africa and around the world: OpenStax describes the Out of Africa model, in which early humans left Africa around 100,000 years ago and migrated to diverse areas of the world, and the Smithsonian's 'Humans Change the World' timeline records modern humans in Asia between 80,000 and 60,000 years ago, Australia by about 50,000, Europe by about 40,000, and the Americas by about 15,000 years ago.

The first modern humans shared the planet with at least three other hominin species, and as H. sapiens spread, those species — including Homo erectus, the Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis), and Homo floresiensis — became extinct, leaving modern humans the sole survivor of the hominin family tree; the Smithsonian timeline dates the Neanderthal extinction to about 28,000 years ago, while OpenStax estimates 35,000 to 50,000 years ago.

Genetic evidence shows that Homo sapiens and Neanderthals interbred where their ranges overlapped: the Smithsonian reports Neanderthal DNA makes up about 1–4% of the genomes of present-day people with non-African ancestry, OpenStax reports about 2.3–2.6% for people of East Asian descent, interbreeding events go back more than 100,000 years with gene flow in both directions, and most of the modern human genome still derives from Africa.

Homo sapiens developed symbolic culture, art, and complex language: humans recorded information on objects by about 77,000 years ago, made permanent drawings between about 60,000 and 40,000 years ago, and created art, music, personal adornment, rituals, and a complex symbolic world; around 40,000 years ago there was a marked change in tool technology, subsistence, and symbolic expression across Africa, Asia, Europe, and Australia; spoken language does not fossilize, so its origin is uncertain.

All living humans are one species — Homo sapiens, living worldwide — and the species is young: genetic variation among living human populations is small and greatest in Africa, consistent with a recent African origin, while relative to millions of years of hominin evolution our species is young; the Smithsonian lists open questions such as the identity of our direct evolutionary ancestor (Homo heidelbergensis is the leading candidate) and the full extent of interbreeding, so the story is still being written.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Date of the emergence of Homo sapiens.
positions: The Smithsonian's Homo sapiens species page dates the evolution of the species to about 300,000 years ago in Africa.

OpenStax's Introduction to Anthropology (5.3) dates the first appearance of modern H. sapiens to about 200,000 years ago in Africa; the Smithsonian's own 'Humans Change the World' page uses the 200,000-year figure, and the Smithsonian's 'One Species, Living Worldwide' page notes its video has not been updated to the 300,000-year date.
OpenStax (5.4) describes the consensus Out of Africa model as tracing living humans to a population in Africa about 200,000 years ago.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both sources agree the origin is African. The lesson brackets the dates ('roughly 200,000 to 300,000 years ago') and attributes each figure to its source; no single date is asserted as exact.

positions: The Smithsonian's 'Humans Change the World' timeline lists 'By 28,000 years ago: Extinction! Neanderthals become extinct.'
OpenStax (5.3) states the Neanderthals went extinct around 35,000 to 50,000 years ago.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the range with attribution ('the Smithsonian dates their extinction to about 28,000 years ago, while OpenStax gives a wider estimate of 35,000 to 50,000 years ago') and avoids pinning a single figure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Amount of Neanderthal DNA in modern genomes.
positions: The Smithsonian's Ancient DNA and Neanderthals page reports Neanderthal contributions of about 1–4% of the genomes of non-African modern humans, and up to 6–9% in modern humans who lived about 40,000 years ago.
OpenStax (5.3) reports the genetic evidence is most prominent in people of East Asian descent, accounting for between 2.3% and 2.6% of their DNA.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The figures are consistent (the East Asian figure sits inside the 1–4% range). The lesson states the 1–4% range with Smithsonian attribution and mentions the East Asian figure as an example; no exact figure is asserted beyond the sources.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No machine-generated draft existed for this topic in public/content/phase-4/lessons.json, so there were no draft claims to audit.
correctionsNeeded: Attributed-date discipline: every date in the lesson carries its source (Smithsonian vs OpenStax), and the emergence date is bracketed rather than asserted as a single figure.

The interbreeding note is kept to the factual, attributed statement that some interbreeding occurred (1–4% Neanderthal DNA in non-African genomes per Smithsonian); genetics depth is explicitly left to the biology subject.
The lesson avoids claiming a single cause for the Neanderthal extinction; the sources present multiple hypotheses, and the lesson says so.
rightsIssues: All sources used REFERENCE_ONLY; facts were synthesized into original prose, and no source wording was reproduced beyond short attributed phrases.

sourceRecords.title: Homo sapiens — Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Reuses the id already registered in the phase-4 source registry with an identical URL. Supports: the working definition (Homo sapiens is the species that you and all other living human beings on this planet belong to); evolution in Africa about 300,000 years ago during dramatic climate change; anatomical features of anatomically modern humans (brain averaging about 1300 cc, high-vaulted skull, flat near-vertical forehead, reduced brow ridges, lighter skeleton); specialized tools (composite tools, fishhooks, harpoons, bows and arrows, spear throwers, sewing needles); art, music, personal adornment, rituals, and a complex symbolic world; spread to every continent; open questions (direct ancestor, extent of interbreeding). Facts synthesized in original wording; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Ancient DNA and Neanderthals — Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. New id minted (not in phase-2/phase-4 registries). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: Neanderthals as our closest extinct relatives; divergence of the Neanderthal and modern human lineages around 500,000 years ago, with Neanderthals evolving outside Africa; shared habitats with modern humans in the Middle East and Europe; interbreeding (introgression) between Homo sapiens and Homo neanderthalensis; Neanderthal DNA contributing about 1-4% of the genomes of non-African modern humans; gene flow in both directions including early gene flow into the Neanderthal genome about 100,000 years ago; most of the modern human genome deriving from Africa; Denisovans contributing up to 4-6% of the genome of modern humans in certain regions. Used REFERENCE_ONLY; facts synthesized in original wording; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Language & Symbols — Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. New id minted (not in phase-2/phase-4 registries). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: use of ocher and manganese to mark objects by 350,000 years ago; burials with beads and symbolic objects by 100,000 years ago; personal adornment expressing identity by 100,000 years ago; recording information on objects by 77,000 years ago; two- and three-dimensional images by 40,000 years ago and all major representational techniques by 17,000 years ago; symbols for words and concepts by around 8,000 years ago with true writing developing over the following millennia; the statement that spoken language does not fossilize, so scientists are not sure when complex spoken language began. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
